title: Orchestrator slimming, prefetch policy redesign, and KV-cache coordinator rewrite
creator: Amira Patel
description: This ticket captures a cross-cutting refactor to reduce tail latency and CPU contention caused by the monolithic request orchestrator and the current KV-cache coordinator. Two related pain-points were observed in production: (1) periodic full-scan prefetches and conservative eviction heuristics that amplify p99 latency during traffic spikes, and (2) a single global scheduler/lock that serializes batcher handoff and increases jitter under high concurrency. The goal is to split responsibilities, replace aggressive synchronous scans with an incremental prefetch policy, and rewrite the coordinator to a shard-aware, event-driven component with explicit backpressure signals.
background: Over the last six months we've seen recurring latency spikes when autoscaling events or bursty workloads arrive. Postmortems and flamegraphs point at: hotspots in the orchestrator's request-routing path, synchronous KV-store scans triggered by prefetch heuristics, and a coarse-grained scheduler mutex that serializes slot allocation. Existing mitigations (increase threadpool size, bump backoff) are brittle and raise cost. Benchmarks on synthetic workloads show p99 token latency increases of 2.3x under 3x traffic bursts compared to steady-state. The service currently depends on crossbeam 0.8 and tokio 1.12; some internal components use blocking Mutex guards across async boundaries which complicates refactors.
proposed_solution:
1) Introduce a lightweight per-shard coordinator that manages KV cache lifecycle: warmup, incremental compaction, and eviction. The coordinator will expose a non-blocking API to request prefetched keys and enforce per-shard rate limits.
2) Replace global orchestrator lock with a lockless handoff using per-lane MPSC queues and an ownership token for slot allocation.
3) Rework prefetch policy: move from synchronous full-window scans to predictive incremental prefetch driven by recent token access patterns and a small ML-based predictor (simple LRU+decay model). Provide knobs for aggressiveness and an opt-out for latency-sensitive customers.
4) Upgrade runtime dependencies that block non-blocking rewrite: tokio 1.12 -> 1.22 and crossbeam 0.8 -> 0.9 to get faster channel primitives and better waker behaviour. Ensure no API regressions via integration tests.
5) Add observability counters and traces: per-shard prefetch rate, eviction counts, scan duration, scheduler queue depth, and handoff latency to track regressions and improvements.
tradeoffs:
- Moving to per-shard coordinators increases code surface area and adds a small memory overhead for per-shard metadata, but reduces contention and isolates noisy tenants.
- Introducing an ML-based predictor adds operational complexity; we start with a simple decay-based heuristic and isolate the predictor behind a feature flag.
- Dependency upgrades carry risk of subtle async behaviour changes; to mitigate, we will run long-lived canary instances and a dedicated integration test cluster.
acceptance_criteria: p50 token latency unchanged or improved on steady-state traffic
p95 token latency improved by >=15% on bursty synthetic workload
p99 token latency improved by >=25% on bursty synthetic workload
KV full-scan rate reduced by >=85% in production traces
Scheduler lock contention metric reduced to near-zero (no global mutex stalls observed in flamegraphs)
End-to-end integration tests (benchmarks + long-running canary) pass for 72 hours
Docs updated: architecture note + runtime knobs (prefetch.aggressiveness, coordinator.mode)
Migration plan validated and code reviewed by runtime and infra owners
